label: What We Did Not Touch
notes: The closing chapter is a map of exits rather than a new construction. Tell students that every frontier here grows out of one habit they already own: the cross-ratio, the bracket determinant, or the absolute conic. The course gave them the dialect; this lecture shows the countries where it is spoken next.

label: Translation Guide
notes: Frame the whole chapter as a translation table. Diagrams stop being the final answer and become carriers of algebraic state. Each frontier reuses a familiar object: determinants become chirotopes, conics become algebraic curves, the line CP1 becomes a qubit. Stress that the translation is the lesson, not any single new theorem.

label: Map of Frontiers
notes: Walk the hub-and-spoke figure slowly. The core triple of cross-ratio, brackets, and absolute conic sits at the centre, and each spoke is one section of the chapter. Ask students to name, for each spoke, which central tool is being extended before you reveal it. The map is the spine of the lecture.

label: Finite Fields and Coding
notes: Projective planes over finite fields are tiny, complete, and combinatorial. The Fano plane has seven points and seven lines with three points on each. Connect this to coding theory and designs, and note that the cross-ratio still makes sense over any field. This is the most accessible frontier for a first independent project.

label: Higher Dimensions and Grassmannians
notes: Lines in space are the first object beyond points and planes. Plucker coordinates turn a line into six numbers, one bracket per coordinate pair, satisfying a single quadratic relation. That relation is the Klein quadric, so the set of lines becomes a four-dimensional quadric in five-dimensional projective space. Emphasise that brackets are doing the work.

label: The Klein Quadric Teaser
notes: This is the concrete teaser. Spell out the Plucker map and the alternating relation that the six coordinates must satisfy. Two lines meet exactly when a bilinear pairing of their coordinates vanishes, which is incidence rewritten as a single equation. Have students verify the relation on the two example lines drawn on the slide.

label: Algebraic Curves and Bezout
notes: Past conics, a curve is just a homogeneous polynomial of some degree. Bezout says two curves of degrees m and n meet in exactly m times n points once you count complex points, points at infinity, and multiplicity. Use the line-against-cubic check: three roots generically, a double root at a tangency. Multiplicity is non-negotiable.

label: Cubics, Hessian, Duality
notes: The smooth cubic is the richest small example. Its nine inflection points are the common zeros of the curve and its Hessian, and they organise the Cayley-Bacharach phenomenon and the group law on an elliptic curve. The gradient at each point gives a tangent line, and tracing those lines sweeps out the dual curve. Connect duality back to brackets.

label: Oriented and Real Projective Geometry
notes: Oriented projective geometry keeps the sign of the determinant that the projective version throws away. An oriented matroid records, for every triple, whether the bracket is positive, negative, or zero. Zeros still mean incidence; signs remember which side. The Grassmann-Plucker relations constrain those signs, and deciding realizability is genuinely hard.

label: Complex Points and Quantum States
notes: The complex points were always there, hiding the absolute conic and circular points. Made explicit, a qubit is a point of CP1 on the Bloch sphere, two qubits live in CP3, and entanglement is a projective invariant: the determinant of the amplitude matrix vanishes exactly on product states and is preserved by local unitaries. Invariant theory is the doorway.

label: Tropical and Dynamic Geometry
notes: Two motion-and-degeneracy frontiers. Tropical geometry replaces plus and times with min and plus, turning curves into piecewise-linear graphs while keeping Bezout-style counts. Dynamic geometry treats construction primitives as multivalued relations; a line meets a circle in two points, and following branches through complex detours avoids the tangency where they collide.

label: A Map of Frontiers, Recapped
notes: Close by collapsing everything back to the centre. Each frontier extends one tool: brackets to Plucker coordinates and chirotopes, conics to algebraic curves and dual curves, the cross-ratio to finite fields, the absolute conic to the complex and quantum worlds. Send students off with one concrete next step they can compute themselves this week.
